The phrase "I should" can quietly make a decision for you before you've really examined it.

Maybe you should pursue the promotion, buy the house, or follow the career path everyone expects. Some of those choices may genuinely fit your life, but an expectation you've carried for years isn't automatically a priority you've chosen.

Explore what's influencing your decisions with Decision Untangler: https://decisionuntangler.garrettsdevdesk.com

Not every "I should" is an expectation you need to question or discard.

Some reflect commitments you've willingly made, people who depend on you, or responsibilities you genuinely value. Those considerations belong in a thoughtful decision.

The useful exercise is to identify what sits behind the obligation. Ask yourself whether it reflects something important to you and whether your circumstances still support it.

Here's a small exercise for your next difficult decision: Finish the sentence "I should choose this because..."

Write down your answer without editing it. Then look at the reason you've given. Does it reflect a responsibility, a personal value, a practical need, or an expectation you've never really examined?

Decision Untangler helps you work through questions like these: https://decisionuntangler.garrettsdevdesk.com

Two decisions can feel equally obligatory while coming from very different places.

"I should follow through because I made a commitment" may reflect a value you want to honor. "I should do this because people will wonder why I didn't" may reflect social pressure.

Try writing down the reasons behind your strongest obligations. Seeing them in your own words can help you decide how much weight each deserves.

It's surprisingly easy to inherit someone else's definition of success.

A certain salary, job title, home, or lifestyle can become a goal simply because it's what successful adulthood is supposed to look like. Those things may be worthwhile, but you deserve to examine whether they're worthwhile to you.

Decision Untangler helps you reflect on the priorities behind your choices: https://decisionuntangler.garrettsdevdesk.com

The next time "I should" appears in your thinking, ask it to finish the sentence.

What comes after "because" might reveal a commitment you care deeply about, a practical responsibility, or an expectation you've been carrying without realizing it. Each deserves a thoughtful response.

Have you ever questioned something you thought you were supposed to do and discovered that you didn't actually want it?
